title: Siheung Oido Museum: A Beginner's Guide to Korea's Shell-Mound Museum and K-Drama Filming Spot
html:
Most visitors to Korea never make it out to Oido, a small former island in Siheung, Gyeonggi-do, about an hour outside Seoul. But if you're a K-drama fan, or just curious about Korea's ancient history, the Siheung Oido Museum is a quietly fascinating stop — it's both a real archaeological site from the Stone Age and the actual filming location for one of the most-loved K-dramas of the last few years. Here's what it is, why drama fans love it, and how to get there.

What Is Siheung Oido Museum?

Until about 100 years ago, Oido really was an island, cut off from the mainland by the sea. It became connected to the rest of Siheung after large land and causeway projects — the Gunja Salt Farm and the Sihwa Embankment (a sea wall built to reclaim land) — filled in the water around it. Long before any of that, though, Stone Age people were already living here, and the shell mounds they left behind (basically ancient trash heaps full of shells, bones, and broken tools) turned out to be the largest shell-mound site on Korea's west coast. The whole island is now protected as Historic Site No. 441. Inside the museum, you'll find exhibits and hands-on activities about what daily life looked like for these Neolithic (late Stone Age) communities thousands of years ago.

Photo: Siheung Oido Museum exhibition hall, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

Drama Fans: The "Our Beloved Summer" Back-Hug Spot

If the building looks familiar, it's probably from "Our Beloved Summer" (그 해 우리는), the hit 2021–2022 K-drama starring Choi Woo-sik and Kim Da-mi. The show used almost every corner of this museum as a filming set — the outdoor plaza, the exhibition hall, and most famously, the long bridge-like walkway outside the building, lined with rows of pillars. That walkway is where the main characters, Kook Yeon-su and Choi Ung, shared the drama's iconic "back hug" scene. Fans will even find a small floor sticker marking the exact spot, with the drama's name written on it, so it's a popular (and free) photo stop even if you've never seen the show.

Photo: The pillared walkway outside Siheung Oido Museum, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

Good to Know Before You Go

The museum is open 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM (last admission 5:30 PM), and closed on Mondays, January 1st, and the Lunar New Year (Seollal) and Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) holidays. The main permanent exhibition hall (3rd floor) is free to enter. There's also a separate, ticketed children's experience room (2nd floor): 1,000 KRW per person for ages roughly 3–64, with discounted group/local-resident rates, and it's free for toddlers under 3 and seniors 65+. That room runs in timed sessions (around 10:30, 13:30, and 15:30) and usually needs advance reservation, so if you're traveling with kids, it's worth calling ahead (+82-31-310-3052) to check availability — the booking site is Korean-only. There's free on-site parking as well. Prices and hours can shift, so it's worth a quick double-check on the official site (oidomuseum.siheung.go.kr) close to your travel date.

Photo: Outdoor plaza at Siheung Oido Museum, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

How to Get There

The easiest way in is by subway: take Seoul Subway Line 4 (the light-blue line) all the way to its southwestern end at Oido Station — the Suin-Bundang Line also stops here, sharing the same platform. From central Seoul, expect roughly 1 to 1.5 hours depending on where you start. The museum itself isn't within easy walking distance of the station, so from Oido Station it's simplest to take a short taxi (just a few minutes), or check Naver Map or Kakao Map for the current local bus route, since bus numbers can change. One thing a lot of Korean visitors do: pair the museum with a stop at Oido's seafood town right on the water, where stalls grill fresh clams and shellfish fresh off the mudflats — it's a well-known local food outing, not just a tourist thing, so if you have time after the museum, it's worth the short trip over.

Photo: The grounds around Siheung Oido Museum, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

💬 Visiting for the drama filming spot, the history, or both? Let us know in the comments — happy to help you plan the trip out!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Siheung Oido Museum: a Neolithic shell-mound site and the real Our Beloved Summer filming spot near Seoul.
